content.thinking: Since there's no actual data available, I need to avoid fabricating root causes or impact figures. I'll keep the executive summary in plain language, referring to "an internal service" rather than naming components, and clearly list out any assumptions instead of stating unverified numbers.

assumptions: That the alert itself was accurate — that the service really was returning elevated errors — is assumed, not confirmed, since no metrics could be read to corroborate it.
That the problem was ongoing at escalation is an assumption drawn from the absence of a recovery signal, not from an observed unhealthy state.

The absence of recent feature flag changes was read from the flag provider and taken to rule out a flag-driven cause; no other class of change (deploys, infrastructure, upstream dependencies) was checked.

The empty metrics read was treated as a data-availability problem rather than as evidence about the service; it is possible the same fault affected both the service and its telemetry, but that was not investigated.
No logs were read, so nothing about the nature of the errors — which endpoints, which callers, which failure mode — is known.
input.executive_summary: An automated alert reported that one of our internal services had started returning an unusually high share of errors. The automated responder picked the alert up immediately and tried to gather the service's recent performance data to work out what was wrong, but no data came back, and a check of recent configuration changes turned up nothing. With no evidence to work from, the responder handed the incident to on-call engineers rather than attempt a fix. Because the underlying data was unavailable, we cannot say how many customers or requests were affected, how bad the error rate was, or when the problem started or ended; the service had not been observed to recover by the time the available records end. The only action taken during the automated phase was the escalation itself — no change was made to the service.
input.root_cause: Unknown. An elevated error rate alert fired for io-shop, but no per-minute metrics could be retrieved for the incident window and the feature flag provider showed no recent changes, so the automated investigation produced no supported hypothesis and the incident was escalated to humans without a cause being identified.
